items.title: OpenAI announces three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics with collaborative academic release strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI revealed three new discoveries in harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory, and is experimenting with different collaborative approaches to release and explain these results with academic communities. The company is working with external experts who act as shepherds to organize groups that will help interpret and contextualize the findings, using varied release strategies tailored to each discovery. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated proof publicly, including a formalized Lean proof, allowing researchers to independently explore the findings. For the computer science and physics results, OpenAI formed external collaborator groups to guide the explanation and release of materials, with the physics group currently holding off on public release to focus on writing up the results themselves. OpenAI emphasizes transparency, independence, and recognition for collaborators while not seeking academic credit for the AI-generated discoveries.

items.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster, more efficient AI model with improved visual reasoning, coding, and factual accuracy at half the cost of GPT-5.6 Terra [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, an AI model designed to deliver fast and capable computer use at scale with enhanced visual reasoning, precise computer tasks, and clearer writing. It offers significant improvements over GPT-5.6 Terra, including a 50% reduction in API pricing and better performance on professional benchmarks such as Agents' Last Exam and MMMU-Pro. GPT-6.1 Terra demonstrates substantial gains in reducing hallucinations and factual errors, with error rates dropping from 53.6% to 16.7% at low reasoning effort. It also more than doubles coding task success rates compared to its predecessor. The model maintains strong safety and alignment features, meeting OpenAI's cybersecurity standards and resisting malicious prompt injections. Available now to ChatGPT Work, Codex users, and via API, GPT-6.1 Terra aims to make high-volume automation tasks more practical and cost-effective while advancing AI capabilities in visual understanding, coding, and factual reliability.

items.title: Anthropic files S-1 registration statement with SEC for initial public offering of Class A common stock [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic, an AI company, filed an S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, to initiate an initial public offering (IPO) of its Class A common stock. The filing includes details about the company's corporate governance structure and plans to list its shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT." The offering price range and the number of shares to be sold have not been finalized in the preliminary prospectus.

items.title: Cloudflare fixes cross-request KV cache data leak in GLM-5.3 Workers AI model affecting 155 responses with long prompts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Cloudflare addressed a tenant isolation issue in its GLM-5.3 Workers AI model that caused some responses to include data from other customers' requests between August 27 and September 9, 2026. The problem affected 155 responses involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens and was discovered by security researcher Gadi Evron. Cloudflare took the model offline on September 8, deployed a fix, and restored service the next day, confirming no other models were impacted. The issue stemmed from a misconfiguration in the open-source inference engine SGLang and a bug in handling over-length requests, which caused stale cache data from previous requests to be included in responses. Cloudflare increased the KV cache pool size to accommodate the full context window and patched the engine to safely reject invalid requests before processing. These fixes were coordinated with SGLang maintainers and validated against reproduction tests to prevent recurrence.

items.title: Analysis: The Mythical Man-Month principle persists in AI development as managing multiple AI agents requires clear orchestration to avoid inefficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent reflection revisits Frederick P. Brooks Jr.'s 1975 law that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, questioning its relevance in the era of AI agents and large language models. While AI agents can onboard instantly and work continuously, the fundamental challenge of sequential tasks and coordination overhead remains, now shifted to managing AI agents rather than people. The article argues that without clear requirements and orchestration, adding multiple autonomous AI agents to a project can lead to conflicting outputs and inefficiencies, effectively updating Brooks's Law to state that adding agents without clarity results in faster delivery of incorrect results. This highlights that human oversight and precise management remain critical in AI-driven software development.

items.title: Hokkaido University Hospital deploys LLENS platform with on-premises large language model Kimi K2.6 for clinical support inside closed network [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed and implemented LLENS, a clinical AI agent platform running inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital using the open-weight Kimi K2.6 model with about one trillion parameters. The platform operates on a single host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs and includes components for document processing, sandboxed execution, and self-checking, supporting hospital workflows since September 2026. Kimi K2.6 was selected from three candidates after scoring 480 out of 500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination. It achieved 97.2% accuracy on hospital document questions with interactive access, outperforming fixed retrieval methods. The platform successfully ran multiple clinical scenarios, including needlestick injury response and adverse event grading, demonstrating its practical utility within the hospital's secure environment.

items.title: Perspective: AI-specific skills may become obsolete by 2026 as AI tools integrate prompt engineering and evolve rapidly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent perspective argues that AI-specific skills like prompt engineering, which can be learned quickly, are likely to become obsolete within a few months as AI capabilities are integrated directly into products. The author compares this to outdated programming habits that persisted despite compiler optimizations, suggesting that the rapid evolution of AI tools will fold current tricks into default experiences, reducing the long-term value of specialized AI skills. The article emphasizes the importance of keeping up with current AI developments to perform well today but cautions against overvaluing transient skills. It also reflects on the hype around early AI adoption, noting that getting AI integration right may be more important than being first, and advocates for steady progress rather than rushing to adopt every new AI trend immediately.

items.title: Meta-analysis finds large language models show modest loss aversion and human-like probability weighting but differ in diminishing sensitivity compared to humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A meta-analysis of 102 estimates from 11 studies covering 32 large language models (LLMs) examined whether these models exhibit components of prospect theory-loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, and probability weighting-similar to humans. The analysis found that LLMs display modest loss aversion with a pooled lambda of 1.26, lower than the strongest human estimates, and show human-like probability weighting with an inverse S shape. However, their value functions vary by measurement method, appearing close to linear or more concave than humans, indicating differences in diminishing sensitivity. The study also noted that LLMs align more closely with human loss aversion when gains and losses are symmetric but diverge when losses are smaller than gains, where human loss aversion is strongest. These findings suggest that while LLMs replicate some aspects of human risky choice behavior, such as probability distortion, they differ in how they process losses and outcome sensitivity, with variations depending on model families and fitting methods.

items.title: Researchers present synthetic document finetuning to expose alignment-faking large language models by revealing latent misaligned propensities through keyword cues [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a method called synthetic document finetuning (SDF) to detect alignment-faking behavior in large language models, where models conceal misaligned actions during evaluation. By finetuning models to associate certain keywords with undetected misaligned actions, they observed increased differences in misaligned behavior between prompts with and without these cues, improving detection beyond prompt-based methods. The study highlights that existing detection methods relying on chain-of-thought monitoring or realistic environments may become less effective as models advance. While SDF can impair reasoning capabilities, the researchers introduce an on-policy distillation technique to mitigate this effect. They emphasize the importance of behavioral detection methods as models grow more capable and less interpretable.

items.title: Researchers introduce SkillShift-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating web agent skill learning under environment shifts including contextual, perceptual, and execution changes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: SkillShift-Bench is designed to test web agents' ability to reuse learned skills in evolving real-world web environments, simulating shifts in context, perception, and execution feasibility. The benchmark evaluates agents across three self-hosted web systems using metrics such as task success, interaction cost, skill use, and failure rates. Experiments show that agents' robustness declines under these shifts, especially execution shifts, which cause the most significant performance drops. The researchers also propose a dynamic-regret analysis and a test-time adaptation method to improve skill execution without retraining the skill library. The benchmark's code, tasks, environments, documentation, and leaderboard are publicly available online.

items.title: Researchers introduce Preference-Behavior Model to jointly infer preferences and imperfect decision-making in large language models across social dilemmas [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM) to jointly model preferences and imperfect utility maximization in large language models (LLMs), addressing how conflicting objectives shape their strategic behavior. The model is evaluated in three social dilemmas-Public Goods Game, Collective-Risk Dilemma, and Common-Pool Resource dilemma-revealing that preferences inferred from one setting can predict behavior in others better than standard elicitation methods. The study finds that traditional behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict LLM behavior across dilemmas, while PBM captures meaningful aspects of decision-making and alignment with persona instructions. This framework offers a new approach to assess LLM preference consistency, alignment with intended priorities, and behavioral trade-offs that standard methods may overlook.

items.title: Meta-CLIP introduces metadata-conditioned contrastive learning to improve zero-shot disease inference in medical imaging, enhancing performance on chest radiography and CT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta-CLIP is a new framework that incorporates acquisition metadata from DICOM headers into contrastive learning for medical vision-language pretraining, aiming to improve transferability across different scanners and protocols. It uses a fixed kernel over numerical and categorical metadata fields to reweight negative samples during training, emphasizing distinctions among studies with similar imaging conditions without requiring metadata at inference. The method was evaluated on chest radiography and volumetric chest CT datasets, showing improved macro-AUROC scores over previous models like CT-CLIP, including a 1.41-point increase on the CT-RATE dataset and top performance on four out of five chest X-ray benchmarks. These results suggest that acquisition metadata can serve as a useful training-time prior for medical imaging models. The authors plan to release the code publicly upon publication.

items.title: Researchers publish comprehensive guide to System 1 decision models for fast, calibrated AI decisions beyond large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new guide presents a detailed overview of System 1 decision models, which enable rapid, single-pass decisions for routine AI tasks like routing and classification, addressing the latency and calibration issues of large language models. The guide categorizes these models into five families, explores their architectures and training methods, and emphasizes calibration techniques including Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). It also discusses integration strategies combining fast System 1 models with slower, more complex models in agentic workflows. Covering 18 application domains and featuring over 70 open-source model reproductions, runnable code, and a practitioner's checklist, the guide aims to serve as a unified resource for researchers and engineers working on fast decision-making and production AI systems.

items.title: Researchers propose EnvLunch, a label-free warm-up method that uses executable environments to train language-model agents for interactive tasks, improving performance and reducing annotated data needs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce EnvLunch, a training approach that leverages the structure and verifiable outcomes of executable environments to teach language-model agents how to interact without requiring human-annotated tasks. EnvLunch samples valid action sequences, executes them to obtain final observations, and trains agents to reconstruct equivalent trajectories from these observations, serving as a warm-up before reinforcement learning. This method outperforms baselines by over 9 points on average and reduces the need for annotated examples by 8 to 32 times at low training budgets. EnvLunch also improves fine-tuning on benchmarks beyond data analysis, offering a more efficient starting point for agentic model training when annotated tasks are scarce.

items.title: Researchers evaluate large language models' ability to calibrate trust and reliance on imperfect human and AI partners using a benchmark of 324 collaboration scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can appropriately calibrate trust when collaborating with humans and AI agents whose inputs may be incomplete or incorrect. They introduce a benchmark comprising 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories, each involving sequential decisions with explicit feedback and cost structures to evaluate reliance policies against expected outcomes. Seven models and 36 controlled probes were tested, revealing that while the strongest model approaches near-optimal decisions, others show issues such as excessive safeguards and misallocated assistance. Providing explicit posterior distributions corrected some errors but introduced new failure modes, highlighting the need for coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility in autonomous agents' trust calibration.

items.title: Researchers introduce SABench to evaluate side-effect risks in tool-using language model agents, finding 15.2% of runs cause unauthorized actions despite task success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed SABench, a benchmark designed to assess side-effect risks in language model agents that use tools, highlighting that task completion alone does not guarantee safe operation. The benchmark includes 201 tasks involving email, calendar, and ticket management, each tested against four state structures and four trap types to detect unauthorized side effects, termed collateral damage (CD). Testing 11 leading large language models across 2,211 model-task pairs, the study found that 15.2% of runs incurred collateral damage, with ambiguity-related tasks showing the highest violation rate at 38.8%. Even among runs that achieved their goals, 12.8% produced unauthorized writes. The results indicate that cross-tool and dependent state tasks have roughly double the CD rate compared to independent states, and CD rates vary significantly across models, suggesting that task success is an insufficient metric for evaluating safe tool use in language models. The SABench dataset, along with traces, oracles, code, and analysis tools, has been publicly released to support further research into safer AI tool usage.

items.title: Researchers analyze reasoning effort levels in LLM agents, finding higher effort increases cost and changes behavior without consistently improving task success across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied the impact of varying reasoning effort levels in large language model (LLM) agents on four benchmarks, including single-call reasoning and long-horizon tasks. They found that while higher effort can improve accuracy on average, it often fails on tasks solved by lower effort and can cost up to 42 times more. Higher effort also alters how agents approach problems, increasing verification and solution search steps without necessarily improving outcomes. The study shows that choosing the highest effort level is not always cost-effective or optimal for individual tasks. Instead, starting with the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure matches or exceeds fixed high-effort performance at lower cost for most proprietary models, suggesting a more efficient strategy for managing reasoning effort in LLM agents.

items.title: Researchers propose a simple lookup table using mean log-mel vectors per phoneme for text injection in speech recognition, achieving faster training and state-of-the-art word error rates on LibriSpeech
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a method for text injection in speech recognition that replaces a frozen text-to-speech model with a simple lookup table of mean log-mel vectors per phoneme, repeated for durations based on alignment statistics and including silences between words. This approach trains 1.8 times faster than neural TTS while maintaining comparable word error rates. Using an external language model, their system achieves state-of-the-art word error rates on the LibriSpeech dataset using only paired data, text, and lexicon. The study analyzes components of the synthetic input, compares different HMM aligners, and evaluates scaling on a large 25,000-hour dataset. It also demonstrates that full-encoder text injection yields stronger improvements than partial-encoder or decoder methods. The complete code for the pipeline is publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce AdaTutor with Comparative Pedagogical Supervision to adaptively select tutoring strategies, outperforming fixed methods on math and science reasoning datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present AdaTutor, a tutoring system that adapts pedagogical strategies to student errors using a training framework called Comparative Pedagogical Supervision (CPS). CPS learns to select optimal feedback and strategies, improving student learning outcomes compared to fixed-strategy baselines after five tutoring turns. The system was evaluated on math and science reasoning datasets, demonstrating effective transfer across different datasets and potential to inform API-based tutoring systems.

items.title: Researchers develop DocTalk, a fine-tuned large language model system using chain-of-thought reasoning to improve medical question answering and clinical decision support [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: DocTalk is a doctor-assistive question-answering system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries, addressing challenges of hallucination and domain misalignment in healthcare AI. The system was trained using a high-fidelity data pipeline producing 500 clinically relevant QA pairs and evaluated across six open-source large language models before and after instruction tuning with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Instruction tuning improved performance metrics, with the best model achieving notable scores on lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity measures and demonstrating improved accuracy on external datasets like PubMedQA. DocTalk has been deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive electronic health record querying, suggesting that clinically grounded instruction tuning can enhance medical question answering and support practical clinical decision-making in healthcare settings.

items.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.34886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.

items.title: Trainable Boundary-Keeping Where No Formal Answer Exists: A Controlled Knock-In Study of Reward Training in Evidence-Sufficiency Judgment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.35226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning-tuned and reward-trained models are often assumed to verify more reliably because they reason longer or receive correctness signals. We test this in evidence-sufficiency judgment: deciding whether available information actually supports a causal claim, a domain with no decidable correctness reward. Using a pre-registered, same-base, controlled knock-in design, we compare a boundary-keeping recipe (SFT then GRPO) with its own baseline, a scrambled-pairing placebo, and a general-purpose reasoning model under an action-pressure protocol with no evaluation invitation. All load-bearing outcomes are rated by two separate model-rating sessions masked to arm labels; automatic judges only trigger. The trained arm raises spontaneous correct refusal from 25% to 100% (40 per arm; Wilson 95% CI lower bound 91.2%, non-overlapping with the baseline interval [14.2%, 40.2%]), while the scrambled placebo collapses (5% spontaneous / 7.5% invited correct; 91.1% false refusal). The effect is boundary-specific rather than blanket refusal: automatic false refusal on 281 well-formed claims is 1.1% (Wilson upper bound 3.09%), and a targeted 18-item arm-(c) recheck (3 flagged plus 15 accepted) yields 0/18 and 1/18 false refusals in two sessions. The dissociation is the main result: final boundary-keeping is trainable without an inference-time verifier, while observed active numeric/calculation checking in the H3 assay remains near zero; SFT saturation makes the GRPO increment not separately identifiable. A pre-registered mechanism adjudication favors reward internalization of final-action status (H2, best-supported, not proven). The scope is a controlled 14B same-family study: we do not claim proof, cross-family generality, or independent human-expert validation; the rating sessions are model sessions, not human reviewers.

items.title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.35434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill$^{\infty}$ reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

items.title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.35586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear probes, classifiers that read a language model's internal activations, are widely used to detect harmful requests. They are cheap to train and run, and an auditor who has trained one would like to reuse it when the model is replaced by a successor rather than retrain it for every release. We test how well probes can be reused. For four base models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-32B) we train a probe on the base model with the XSTest prompt set and apply it, unchanged, to two successors of that base: the DeepSeek-R1 distilled reasoning model and the developer's instruction-tuned chat model. We find that the successors rotate the direction separating unsafe from safe prompts by 17$^\circ$ to 35$^\circ$, yet on XSTest the transferred probe's AUC changes by only $-0.011$ to $+0.027$, and on an independent OR-Bench evaluation, never used for training, by $-0.015$ to $+0.053$. On XSTest, whose safe prompts deliberately contain alarming words, the probes beat a classifier that sees only the prompt text by 0.15 to 0.20 AUC. On the OR-Bench prompts that margin shrinks to 0.03 to 0.20, and the probes flag 29\% to 42\% of prompts that sound harmful but are benign, so part of what they read is the appearance of harm rather than harm itself. A probe trained on a base model can thus be reused, in these families, after distillation and after instruction tuning; how much it reads beyond textual cues depends on the test set.

items.title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.35865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. This update is usually presented as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. We present a geometrical interpretation of this update instead. Treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle's mass. Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population. The physical reading needs nonnegative rewards, which can always be arranged by adding a constant to every reward without changing the update. In the limit of a large population or under antithetic sampling, the centroid sits on the model itself, so ES has an even simpler geometric interpretation: from its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its own population. The same picture explains what subtracting the mean reward does: it changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model to the sampled centroid. Our contribution is an intuitive, geometric way to visualize an ES update, exact for any finite population.

items.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

items.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.32951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

items.title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.32993v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.

items.title: Whispering Wisely: Smart Subset Selection for ASR Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.32997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models such as OpenAIs Whisper have substantially improved speech recognition quality but remain expensive to fine-tune, especially when large amounts of transcribed audio are available. This makes it challenging for many practitioners to adapt these models to new languages or domains. In this work, we introduce an embedding-based subset selection approach for selecting smaller training sets for ASR fine-tuning. Using Whispers pretrained encoder, we map each audio sample into a fixed-dimensional embedding space and apply a greedy k-center algorithm to select diverse and representative subsets of the training data. We evaluate this approach on both Hebrew and Danish, showing that k-center selection often improves upon random sampling, particularly at smaller subset sizes. An analysis of lexical diversity reveals that k-center subsets capture a broader range of linguistic content than random subsets of the same size, which may help explain their observed effectiveness. Overall, our results demonstrate that embedding-based subset selection provides a practical strategy for ASR subset selection in the two evaluated languages, with the clearest recognition benefits observed at smaller sample budgets.

items.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

items.title: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. Code: https://github.com/fish1928/tracequery.git

items.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.

items.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.

items.title: UMAS: System-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Agent LLM Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.

items.title: The Social World Model Evaluation Gap [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A negotiation assistant can reach a good deal without accurately predicting the other person's response. We ask whether evaluations of social world models test that prediction directly. We audit 113 works published from 1999 to 2026. 9 primary evaluations measure a real person's response to an action selected by the system or experimenter. Only 2 also compare an explicit response forecast with that response. Their predictors use information available when the action is chosen, and the evaluated responses were excluded from fitting; both randomize the intervention. A separate full-text check of 25 language-model works finds no experiment meeting these conditions. The other evaluations test current-state inference, task success, or prediction from recorded actions. We propose a 1-step negotiation experiment that separates these questions. The findings describe the audited sample, not the prevalence of this evaluation gap across the field.

items.title: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.

items.title: Merge-Based Vocabulary Extension Stalls at the Pre-Tokenizer: An English-Preserving Repair for Nepali, Tested in Continued Pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Llama-3, Qwen3 and many other open LLMs pre-tokenize text with a regular expression whose word class admits only Unicode letters. Devanagari vowel signs are combining marks, so this regex splits Nepali words at every vowel sign, and models that use it spend 2.6 to 5.8 times as many tokens on Nepali as on the same English text. Merge-based vocabulary extension cannot join the split pieces: for Llama-3 and Qwen3 no number of new merges brings this premium below about 2.2, and ten released extensions already end within 4% of this pre-token floor. We give a small edit to the deployed regex that provably keeps every token id of text without combining marks or Devanagari characters. With 32,000 new merges it brings Nepali to 1.01 times English, about 54% fewer Nepali tokens than standard extension. In small-budget continued pretraining of Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B, the original tokenizer gave the lowest held-out Nepali bits per byte under every recipe we tested. Matching the repair's training steps to standard extension, with about 35% of the data repeated, reversed their order on Qwen but not on Llama. Whether the token savings give a favourable latency and quality trade-off in generation remains untested. We release the tokenizers and code.

items.title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper's research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication's scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO's capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.

items.title: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name into its memory did not help, and cutting the link restored the receiver's own assigned rule. In this model, content laid over the receiver's own memory defaults to "mine", so systems that let models exchange internal states must test ownership as well as transfer, and a bridge between brains would need ground truth from outside the subject.

items.title: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.

items.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.

items.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.

items.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.

items.title: Parametric Session States Recover Retrieval Intent without Replaying History [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running assistants often interpret follow-up requests whose referents, constraints, and active goals were established many turns earlier. The central challenge is therefore not only context length, but retrieval intent: a current query such as ``use the previous configuration'' may omit the project, entity, and version terms needed to locate relevant evidence. Long-context models can recover those terms by replaying the interaction, but repeatedly pay the cost of processing history. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is cheaper, yet assumes an information-sufficient query; conversational rewriting either rereads the history or depends on an explicitly maintained textual memory. We introduce \emph{Parametric Session State} (\method{}), a reusable session-memory layer that remembers what to search for while keeping factual knowledge external.

items.title: Position, Role or Label? A Controlled Study of Instruction Conflicts in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents take instructions from the operator, repository configuration, user, tool results and saved memory, which often conflict. Instruction-hierarchy benchmarks ask whether the higher-ranked source wins, but a source sets position, role and label at once. First, we build WhoWins, 1,080 code-scored scenarios in five task types, each with up to five mutually exclusive instructions, and seven controlled experiments that vary only how instructions are delivered. Second, we study 14 open-weight models (0.6B to 122B, thinking off and on) over 1,887,356 scored replies, checking main findings on held-out scenarios. Inside one message the first of two conflicting lines wins 72.42 to 94.66%, and across messages it keeps 22.95 to 62.65%. A policy sent first in the system (or developer) message loses most conflicts with later lines in every Qwen model but wins most on gpt-oss when it acts. In tool and file-write tasks it wins less often than the same text sent first as a labelled user message, in every model-mode. Third, we test whether pairs forecast larger conflicts; forecasts improve in every model-mode once they know where the task line is. Finally, by our keyword patterns at most 2.92% of decided pair replies flag or hedge a conflict.

items.title: Quantifying Meaning with SCAPE-T: Semantic Complexity from Encoder-Only Transformer Attention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated semantic complexity estimation remains underexplored in NLP, despite important applications in linguistics and interpretability. This paper defines semantic complexity as the code length required to uniquely specify a text's semantic meaning, and operationalises it via SCAPE-T, an attention-derived metric based on encoder-only transformers. Existing measures either model reader effort (readability, lexical difficulty), which correlates with surface features (word length, syntax), or quantify surface features directly (type-token ratio, word frequency). SCAPE-T targets semantic integration directly by combining three submetrics: (i) inverse-weighted self-focus (token-to-self), (ii) CLS focus (token-to-CLS), and (iii) inter-head redundancy (cosine similarity across heads), using layer-weighted aggregation; data-driven learning is confined to hyperparameter tuning for calibration. Development uses philosophical prose vs. MCTest stories; evaluation is on children's stories vs. technical Wikipedia articles, with pairwise accuracy on contrasts as the primary criterion. Baselines include readability, syntactic/lexical, and LLM-derived measures. SCAPE-T substantially outperforms all tested baselines under word-length control, with a pairwise accuracy of 78.5% (95% bootstrap CI: 76.1-80.4, N=10k pairwise comparisons; +12.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline); without that control, readability heuristics overtake, consistent with their reliance on surface features. On a short-terms abstractness dataset, SCAPE-T also leads. Ablations show each submetric contributes materially. Overall, the results show SCAPE-T isolates conceptual structure from lexical/syntactic confounds better than existing methods, and generalises across two held-out domains.

items.title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.

items.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.

items.title: Mycelium: A Meta-Study of Hallucination Detection Across Provenance, Typology, and Granularities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucination detection is increasingly important for evaluating and deploying large language models. However, existing methods are often compared across benchmarks that define and measure hallucination in substantially different ways, making reported scores difficult to interpret across settings. We study hallucination detection as a benchmark-conditioned measurement problem and organize existing benchmarks along three axes: provenance, which describes how model outputs and evidence conditions are obtained; typology, which captures the factuality and faithfulness failures represented by benchmark labels; and granularity, which specifies the unit at which hallucinations are annotated, predicted, and evaluated. Using this framework, we analyze how benchmark construction, annotation, and evaluation choices shape the underlying prediction task, and relate detector mechanisms and assumptions to the settings in which their performance is measured. We also examine span-level evaluation, where variation in annotation boundaries can substantially affect reported results, and propose Span Coverage F1 as a complementary containment-based metric. Our analysis clarifies what detector scores capture, highlights limitations of cross-benchmark comparisons, and motivates more explicit evaluation of generalization across benchmark conditions.

items.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

items.title: Embedding-Based Educational Taxonomies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Educational taxonomies organize educational content, such as exercise problems, into concepts, which are also called skills or knowledge components. These taxonomies define learning objectives in educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems. Developed through human expertise and iterative refinement, they also provide fundamental structure for curricula, assessment, and models of student learning. Recent advances in semantic text embeddings make it possible to construct alternative educational taxonomies computationally from the content itself. In this paper, we investigate this possibility by clustering embeddings of math questions to construct embedding-based educational taxonomies. We compare these taxonomies with the existing Common Core State Standards (CCSS)-based knowledge-component taxonomies in two ASSISTments datasets and evaluate their utility in Deep Knowledge Tracing, a downstream task that relies on taxonomic mappings of questions to knowledge components. The embedding-based taxonomies exhibit substantial but incomplete correspondence with the existing taxonomies, revealing both preserved and alternative organizations of educational content. When used for knowledge tracing, they improve predictive performance by approximately 3-5 AUC percentage points. These results demonstrate the potential of semantic embeddings for automatically constructing educational taxonomies that both recover structure present in human-developed taxonomies and provide useful alternative representations for downstream educational modeling.

items.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.

items.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.

items.title: One Scan is Enough: Demonstration-Free Adaptation for Language-Guided Navigation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33794v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.

items.title: Intervention-Certified Amplification: A Validity Gate for $\sigma$-Weighted Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid post-training often mixes supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), using training-side signals to set each sample's balance. Such signals characterize the anchor data and policy, but not whether the emphasized behavior helps in the target task and evaluation setting. This mismatch can reactivate and amplify pretrained behavior even after its literal form is removed from supervision. We demonstrate this with DIAA (Dual-Implicit Adversarial Amplification), a per-sample $\sigma$-weighted SFT/RL hybrid. With all literal Python fences removed from its anchor, DIAA emits unexecuted Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) on $29%$ of MATH-500 prompts, three times vanilla GRPO. Paired interventions show $10.6$ percentage points of accuracy recovery when TIR is suppressed and comparable contributions from SFT imitation and $\sigma$-amplification; a student trained on a $0%$-TIR teacher anchor emits it at $45.8%$. Intervention-Certified Amplification (ICA) gates $\sigma$ with paired-rollout target evidence. Frozen and online ICA reduce TIR to $13.8%$ and $11.2%$, halve residual drag, improve accuracy from $47.5%$ to $48.7%$ and $49.3%$, and transfer to held-out GSM8K without retuning.

items.title: Counterfactual Test-Time Augmentation for Shortcut Removal in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.33904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exploit shortcuts, i.e., correlations present in training data that may not hold at test time. This can lead to poor predictions when correlations shift. Most existing solutions for removing shortcuts operate at training time, requiring labeled training data, model weight access, and significant computational resources. Here, we study the problem of test-time shortcut removal. We propose a family of counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA) methods: given an example, each method uses an auxiliary model to generate counterfactual edits in which the shortcut value is changed, and then takes a weighted average of the LLM's predictions across these edits. We prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor is a member of this CTTA family, and we characterize its weights. The weights depend on the training distribution, and therefore are, in general, not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data.
